newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo carmaker Zastava mulls foreign partner.
newsitem.headline: Yugo carmaker Zastava mulls foreign partner.

text.p: The Yugoslav car manufacturer Zastava of Kragujevac said on Thursday it will decide on a new foreign partner within the next three months, despite some industry scepticism about the company's prospects.
"The talks have narrowed to two from eight potential partners," said Zvonko Osrecki, spokesman of Zastava Group, which comprises 48 subsidiaries.
"Plans are to replace the existing production programme with a new one with the output reaching 150,000 vehicles by the end of the century," he told Reuters.
Local media earlier reported that talks between car maker Zastava and South Korean Hyundai Corp were in the final phase and that a contract was expected to be signed in the second half of February.
Osrecki refused to comment, but said: "One potential partner is from Europe and the other one from the Far East."

Zastava car plant, which produces the small compact Yugo car, was one of the former Yugoslavia's prime hard-currency earners, providing millions of dollars in badly needed cash for the entire group just five years ago.

Hit by the break-up of the former Yugoslav federation, four years of crippling war-related U.N. sanctions, loss of markets and mismanagement, Zastava's car production has slumped to about 10,000 vehicles last year from as much as 200,000 in 1990.
The company, sharing the fate of the entire economy, is looking to foreign investors to give an urgently needed financial transfusion to keep going and to revitalise its production.
"Our system is exhausted. And we must upgrade our outdated technology to renew our range of products and increase productivity," Osrecki said.
But an industry official expressed doubts any foreign partner would be interested to make any kind of deal with Zastava before it clears its outstanding debt.

"It owes 90 million German marks to Italy's Fiat," he said, talking under condition of anonymity. "It must also deliver a few thousand vehicles paid for in 1991. And what about delayed payments to its employees?"
Zastava made contact with many European car producers on possible cooperation but were turned down by France's Peugeot and Renault and Italy's Fiat, the source said.

Another analyst said the state must decide what to do as it is obvious that Yugoslavia, consisting of Serbia and tiny Montenegro, with only about 10.5 million people and a devastated economy, simply cannot sustain car production.
Zastava has set a very optimistic 1997 production target of 30,000 vehicles of which half is to be exported.
"The most crucial issue for any production is money. And prior to any significant foreign capital inflow privatisation is a must," the industry official said.
"It is also very difficult to find someone abroad who would invest in a politically unstable country," the source added.
